Hand the model a PyTorch reference and grade correctness and speed separately.
Tests that lie at random; defend with repetition and quarantine.
A cage with measured bars: no network, no host writes, no endless runs.

recall.answer: Split a software task into context, generation, and selection; scale serial and parallel test-time compute for code; ground edits in executed tests; read KernelBench; trade performance against correctness; write an agent-system interface; profile before optimizing; handle flaky tests; keep hidden tests hidden; sandbox untrusted code; reproduce a run; and roll back a bad change.

keyTerms.definition: 1 - (1 - p)^K; parallel samples raise it even when p is fixed.
T_old / T_new; the ranking among kernels that pass the correctness gate.

recall.answer: Intuition: code is checkable, so the agent should write tests next to edits and let execution decide. Equation: coverage = 1 - (1 - p)^K, speedup = T_old / T_new. Code: a loop of edit, run tests, repair. Observation: parallel samples amortize context cost, and speed without correctness is worth zero.
recall.question: State the four-way link: intuition, equation, code, and observation.

sections.title: Four-way link used in this unit

keyTerms.definition: More repair iterations per attempt; raises p, the per-trajectory solve rate.
More trajectories; raises coverage through the 1 - (1 - p)^K law.
Fraction of issues with at least one good candidate.

recall.answer: Split the job into context (find relevant files), generation (write candidate fixes), and selection (pick the winner). Scale each part on its own axis: serial scaling is more repair iterations per attempt, parallel scaling is more attempts.
recall.question: How does CodeMonkeys split and scale the job?

recall.answer: Break test honesty: the trajectory's own tests are written by the same model that writes the edit, so a weak suite passes a wrong edit and serial iterations polish a bad fix. K trajectories copying one wrong plan make parallel scaling theater.
recall.question: What breaks the scaling axes?

keyTerms.definition: Test voting filters cheaply, then a dedicated trajectory compares survivors with fresh tests.
Of the candidates the filter keeps, how many are actually right.
Of the right candidates, how many the filter keeps.

recall.answer: Sampling makes options, tests rank options, a final chooser picks the winner. The three stages fail differently: sampling can miss, tests can misrank, the chooser can tie-break badly. Fix the stage that loses the most.
recall.question: What are the three stages and how do they fail?

recall.answer: Break filter honesty: generated tests encode the same wrong assumption as the candidates, so the filter keeps the wrong ones confidently. A filter with recall 0 drops every candidate and the search returns nothing.
recall.question: What breaks test-time code search?

keyTerms.definition: Execution injects outside information (the trace) so each iteration can improve.
e' = fix(e, r); maps an edit and its trace to the next edit.
r = run(e, t); the fact (pass, fail, trace) the next draft must respect.

recall.answer: Without execution the model judges its own draft with the prior that wrote it: no new information enters. Execution injects the trace from outside, so each iteration can correct the last.
recall.question: Why does execution ground the repair loop?

recall.answer: Break trace informativeness: a bare AssertionError with no line info makes repair guess and iterations wander. A suite passing everything gives grounding with no signal: single-shot with extra steps.
recall.question: What breaks execution grounding?

keyTerms.definition: Hand the model a PyTorch reference; grade the CUDA/Triton kernel on correctness and speed.
s = T_ref / T_kernel; how many times faster than the reference.
Share of problems both correct and with speedup s >= p.

recall.answer: Two-gate grading: gate one runs the kernel on random inputs against the reference, gate two times both on the same hardware. The split exists because optimizing one gate is easy and optimizing both is hard.
recall.question: How does KernelBench grade a kernel?

recall.answer: Break tolerance honesty: a zero-returning kernel passes when tolerance is absolute and true outputs are near zero. A kernel dispatching to the PyTorch reference inside is correct at speedup 1.0 with zero new work.
recall.question: How can a kernel game KernelBench?

keyTerms.definition: No weight on speed compensates for a wrong answer; gate first, then rank.
Correctness is one; nothing passes it by being fast.
The correct kernels; the choice is argmax speedup over this set.

recall.answer: Gate-then-rank: a wrong kernel in production corrupts results silently, while a slow correct kernel only costs time. The cost of wrongness dominates the cost of slowness. In the toy, kernel C (1.4x, correct) ships over B (1.8x, wrong).
recall.question: Why is the tradeoff lexicographic?

recall.answer: Break input coverage: the tests miss the input class where the winner is wrong, so the gate passes a bad kernel. A kernel correct on tests but wrong on deployment inputs is still wrong; the gate was blind.
recall.question: What breaks the correctness gate?

keyTerms.definition: The law the agent lives under: tools, limits, and the shape of every observation.
Every action goes through the interface, the single place for safety, cost, and observability.
Fixed per tool: (exit code, last 20 lines of stdout, last 20 lines of stderr).

recall.answer: A clear interface makes agent behavior predictable and failures diagnosable. A vague interface makes both impossible. In the toy: tools {run_tests, read_file, write_file, shell}, 30s timeout, 1 GB memory cap.
recall.question: Why does the interface matter?

recall.answer: Break enforcement: a documented-but-unenforced interface lets the agent discover the shell ignores the /task limit and write to the host. A 40-tool interface cannot be learned; every call is a guess.
recall.question: What breaks the agent-system interface?

keyTerms.definition: S = 1 / ((1 - f) + f / s); the unoptimized rest caps everything as s grows.
FLOPs per byte moved; tells whether a part is compute-bound or memory-bound.
A receipt for time: says who spent what; measure first, cut second.

recall.answer: Measure first, cut second. Amdahl's law turns the receipt into a bound: doubling one part cannot beat 1 / (rest + part/2). In the toy the matmul at 60 percent is optimized first.
recall.question: What is the profiling workflow?

recall.answer: Break measurement: a profile on size-32 inputs misleads when deployment uses 4096 and the hotspot moves. A profile with every part at 20 percent has no dominant part; the bound for any single part is weak.
recall.question: What breaks profile-guided optimization?

keyTerms.definition: Lies at random; one lie sends the repair loop to fix fine code.
f: P(fail | code good) per run; false alarm falls as f^r.
Mark a test unreliable after repeated unexplained failures; pay 3x runs for honesty.

recall.answer: Repetition: ask the same question three times and take the majority. The defense costs runs, so apply it only to tests with a flake history. In the toy, 3 reruns cut the false-alarm rate to 0.001.
recall.question: How do you defend against flaky tests?

recall.answer: Break independence: a race failing under load fails all 3 reruns on the loaded machine, condemning good code. A test failing 100 percent on good code is not flaky but wrong; quarantine then hides a bug.
recall.question: What breaks the rerun defense?

keyTerms.definition: The match; the agent may never see its questions.
Any information from H reaching the edit: direct read, test name, cached failure.
With no leakage the visible score is a noisy but unbiased estimate of the hidden score.

recall.answer: Visible tests are the practice field, hidden tests are the match. The agent may train on the field freely, but seeing match questions voids the score. In the toy the visible 1.00 versus hidden 0.85 gap is the leakage-free truth.
recall.question: What is the visible/hidden split?

recall.answer: Break the lock: an engineer pasting a hidden failure into context lets the edit target H and the wall falls. Hidden tests identical to visible ones make the split theater.
recall.question: What breaks hidden-test separation?

keyTerms.definition: A cage with measured bars: the agent is strong inside, harmless outside.
Each layer blocks one failure class: filesystem, network, time, log.
Append-only; makes every action reviewable.

recall.answer: No network, writes only under /task, read-only mount for the repo, wall-clock kill at 60 seconds, every action logged. The delete hits the read-only mount.
recall.question: What are the toy sandbox rules?

recall.answer: Break the kernel: a same-user-namespace privileged helper lets the agent escape. A sandbox with no log holds its bars but nobody can prove what happened inside.
recall.question: What breaks sandboxing?

keyTerms.definition: A receipt for the run: seed, versions, inputs, environment.
Every random draw comes from a seeded generator.
Model, library, and compiler versions pinned; fixes the code paths.

recall.answer: With the receipt (seed 7, torch 2.3.1, CUDA 12.1, same snapshot), a rerun is a replay: byte-identical edits, test outputs matching to 1e-6. Without it, a rerun is a new experiment that looks similar.
recall.question: What makes a rerun a replay?

recall.answer: Break the seed: a library drawing from an unseeded OS source makes the rerun differ mysteriously. A receipt with versions but no seed captures half the randomness; the run still wanders.
recall.question: What breaks reproducibility?

keyTerms.definition: A saved game; load the last good save instead of debugging the corruption.
(m - g) * c; 2 step-runs in the toy when the checkpoint after step 2 is used.
The checkpoint is known-good; everything after it is suspect.

recall.answer: A checkpoint is a saved game. Save after every step that passes its checks. When step 4 of 5 corrupts state, roll back to the checkpoint after step 2 and re-run steps 3 and 4.
recall.question: How does rollback recover from corruption?

recall.answer: Break detection: silent corruption lets 3 more steps build on it, so rollback loses good work too. Checkpoints of memory but not the repo restore half a state, and the halves disagree.
recall.question: What breaks rollback?
